summary:
Lunevra is a free browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. It teaches how real missions are designed by making players live with every choice.

Players fly one connected campaign of three missions on real NASA maps. In Mission 1, they build a relay satellite (its job, rocket, antenna, solar power, science instrument, shielding and orbit) and fly a timed capture burn. In Mission 2, they land a rover at Shackleton Crater on the Moon, or Jezero Crater on Mars, and dig for ice or take core samples. In Mission 3, they send the science home by ordering, compressing and error-checking data packets. Each mission hands its result to the next, so a poor early choice costs the player later.

Before each big decision, a mission analyst forecasts the outcome of the options. Afterwards, a debrief explains why the mission worked or failed, with the formulas behind it. Spacecraft appear as NASA's own 3D models.

It matters because most people only see a finished mission, never the trade-offs between mass, power, cost and risk. The game needs no install or account, runs on ordinary laptops, and has a class mode that fits a whole campaign into a 45-minute lesson.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunevra is a decision-based teaching game: every choice has a cost, and the game shows you why. Players design and fly a complete space mission as one campaign of three linked missions, on real NASA maps. Each mission hands its result to the next: Orbit produces the relay's contact windows, Rover produces the science data packets, and Comms turns what survives the trip home into the final campaign score. Every mission follows the same loop (briefing, design, test, deploy, debrief) and is guided by CAPCOM Whiskers, a cat mission-control guide. Random events change every run, and each debrief explains why the mission worked or failed.

Mission 1, Orbit. The player decides what the satellite is for (pure relay, relay plus hazard camera, or relay plus ice hunter) and picks the rocket (three launcher classes whose payload limits shrink for farther worlds), antenna, solar power, a science instrument modelled on real ones (LRO LROC and LEND, MRO HiRISE and SHARAD, MESSENGER MDIS, Dawn FC), radiation shielding, and the orbit, using sliders or real-mission presets. An assembly bay rebuilds a 3D satellite with every part and shows how it changes mass, fuel, power, and money. A test campaign blocks a launch that is too heavy, over budget, under-powered, or too low. Orbits use two-body Kepler physics and the rocket equation. Then come a timed capture burn and a solar-storm decision, where each response has an exact cost in contact time and score. The orbit sets the relay's contact windows for the next mission.

Mission 2, Rover. The player chooses a landing site and seven rover parts, then drives on terrain built from NASA data, in a 3D view with a 2D fallback. Slopes, shadows, power, and random events test the design, and reaching a crater floor takes a tether or legs and costs real time and energy. The Moon (Shackleton crater) is the main campaign, with objectives such as finding water ice; Mars (Jezero crater) is a bonus campaign where the rover collects core samples. The result becomes the science data packets for Mission 3.

Mission 3, Comms. The player orders the packets, picks compression, and adds a parity check, then encodes bits for the downlink. In the Ground station stage, designed by teammate Jeongha as Operation Deep Link, the player points the Deep Space Network dish that faces the target at the real current hour (Earth turns 15 degrees an hour), locks the sync pulses, picks the spacecraft's signal out of three by ear, and rebuilds the rover's NASA terrain photo tile by tile with majority voting to repair errors. This stage is worth 20 of the mission's 100 points. The player then decodes Earth's reply. Jeongha's full standalone seven-stage version is also in the game. A campaign summary page finally shows how each mission fed the next, with a WHAT / HOW / WHY tree of the whole campaign.

Beyond the Moon and Mars, Mercury, Ceres, and Vesta are orbit challenges on their own NASA maps, so the same design skills are tested in very different gravity.

HOW IT TEACHES

- Forecast, then choose: before the player decides, the game calculates each option's outcome with its own physics and scoring and shows a decision tree. In Orbit it offers three different designs that all pass every go/no-go check, plus the exact contact time and score each solar-storm response would cost. In Comms, it shows three downlink plans with predicted science and noise risk.

- A real trade-off: a relay wants a slow, high pass over the base, while a camera or neutron detector wants to pass low over it. The pixel size of the simulated camera view is computed from the height at which the orbit passes over the landing site, so the picture gets blockier as the orbit rises, and the analyst can offer a sharpest-science design.

- Consequences you can see: consequence chains show how each part changes mass, then fuel, then rocket, power, and money, while the 3D satellite rebuilds in front of the player.

- The debrief explains WHAT happened, HOW and WHY, with a choice -> physics -> result table and the formula behind each row. After each mission, it shows the same table for the player's own run.

- No single perfect answer: automated tests show that different designs can each win and that badly designed ones really fail, so players learn to reason about trade-offs instead of hunting for one recipe.

- Newcomers are supported: hover, focus, or tap any dotted word or "i" badge for a one-line explanation, common space words (periapsis, delta-v, swath, parity) get one automatically on every page, Mission 1 has a guided CAPCOM tutorial that points at each control and waits for the player to try it, and "Ask CAPCOM" answers over 60 questions offline.

- Skills practised: engineering trade-offs (every gain in science or speed costs mass, power, money, or time), decision making under constraints, and teamwork, because a crew agrees on a design and then learns from the outcome.

NASA DATA AND RESOURCES

- Moon: LRO LOLA 87.5 degrees S slope and elevation products (5 m/px) and the Shackleton Rim hillshade give the rover terrain, slopes, and heights. The LRO WAC global mosaic gives the Moon globe. Both come via NASA Moon Trek.

- Mars: MGS MOLA elevation, the MRO CTX Jezero mosaic, and the Viking MDIM global mosaic, via NASA Mars Trek. Mars heights are read from colour, so they are approximate and labelled that way.

- Mercury, Ceres, and Vesta: MESSENGER MDIS and Dawn FC global maps, via NASA Solar System Treks. Dawn's gravity science data gives Ceres's gravity parameter, which sets every orbit there.

- The Moon and Mars globes switch between imagery and laser-altimeter elevation (LRO LOLA, MGS MOLA).

- Planet constants (gravity parameter, radius, day length) come from NASA/JPL, and real-mission orbits (LRO, Gateway NRHO, MRO, MAVEN, MESSENGER, Dawn) are presets, so players can compare their design with real ones.

- NASA 3D Resources models: an assembled satellite from the NASA Satellite Kit that changes with the antenna and solar-wing choice, the Jupiter-C, Atlas, and Saturn V launchers, the real orbiter for each world (LRO, MRO, MESSENGER, Dawn), Perseverance, Opportunity, RASSOR, the Apollo Lunar Module, the Viking lander, and the Deep Space Network dishes and TDRS relay.

- Reference figures from NASA missions: VIPER, RASSOR, TRIDENT, MMRTG, LCROSS (about 5.6% water), Perseverance, and the Deep Space Network.

- Apollo 11 ("The Eagle has landed", "One small step") and Sputnik 1 audio from nasa.gov, and the Voyager Golden Record picture (NASA/JPL-Caltech PIA14113).

- The in-game Briefing Room lists each source with its entry in the NASA Open Data Portal and the licence the catalogue states.

INTENDED IMPACT

Most people only see a finished mission. Lunevra lets students make the trade-offs themselves: more power costs mass, a bigger antenna costs launch capability, a lazy downlink loses science. The goal is for a player to leave a session able to explain why a real mission looks the way it does, and to feel that mission design is something they could do.

It is aimed at ages 12 to first-year university, their teachers, and science clubs. It is free, runs in any modern browser, and needs no install or account. Up to four players share a crew, each with a role (mission lead, engineer, scientist, comms officer), so a class can work as a mission team. Class mode shortens every mission so a whole campaign fits in a 45-minute lesson, and the Briefing Room has a lesson plan, discussion questions, a printable worksheet, and a CSV export of results. Crew profiles, XP, ranks, medals, and decision history are stored only in the browser, so no data leaves the device.

TOOLS

Languages and structure: plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules, with no build step, no framework, and no server needed. Any static web host can run it, and it is hosted on GitHub Pages. Players need only a modern browser, with no special hardware.

3D and graphics: three.js r170 draws the planet globes, the 3D rover view on real terrain, the satellite assembly bay, and the NASA spacecraft models. The models are NASA 3D Resources files in Draco-compressed GLB format, loaded with the three.js GLTFLoader and DRACOLoader. If 3D is unavailable, the game falls back to 2D maps.

Data pipeline: Python scripts (build_terrain.py, build_mars_terrain.py, build_planet_textures.py) rebuild the terrain grids and planet textures from NASA Trek tiles, so anyone can regenerate them from the source data.

Physics and scoring: two-body Kepler orbits and the rocket equation (the same first step NASA's GMAT tool starts from), plus our own models for power, shadow, slopes, link noise, parity error-checking, and cost. The mission analyst's forecasts are computed by the same functions that run the game.

Sound: the ambient score and sound effects are generated live with the Web Audio API. Short public-domain NASA recordings (Apollo 11 and Sputnik 1) play at key moments.

Ask CAPCOM: a question box on every page that matches keywords against the game's built-in notes. It runs entirely offline, with no AI model and no network.

Quality: over 70 automated tests with the Node test runner. They check orbit physics against real missions, contact outages, terrain rules, design limits, Mars rules, the parity code, the ground-station mini-game rules, hand-offs between missions, the NASA model files, the question matcher, and the graphics settings. GitHub Actions runs them on every push.

Optional AI advisor: off by default. A small serverless endpoint (api/advise.js, any OpenAI-compatible provider, for example Groq) can reword a forecast in plain language. It only receives mission numbers, and it never calculates anything. If it is off or unreachable, the game uses its built-in explanations. It is not active on the GitHub Pages site.

AI assistance: much of the code was written with Claude Code and reviewed and tested by the team (see Use of Super Intelligence).

WHAT IS CREATIVE

One campaign, not three mini-games. Mission 1's orbit sets the relay's contact windows, Mission 2's rover produces the science packets, and Mission 3 has to send those packets home. A weak choice early on shows up as a real cost later, which is how mission design feels on a real programme.

Forecast, then choose. Most games show the result after you act. Here the analyst calculates every option first and shows it as a decision tree, so players learn to reason about trade-offs before they commit.

Consequences you can see. The 3D satellite rebuilds with every part you add, consequence chains trace each part through mass, fuel, power, and money, and a simulated camera view gets blockier as the orbit rises. The debrief then lays out WHAT happened, HOW and WHY, with the formula for each row.

No single right answer. Different designs can each win and badly designed ones fail. Mission 1 builds in a genuine conflict: a relay wants a slow, high pass over the base, while a camera wants a low one.

Real hardware and real places. Players see NASA's own models of launchers, orbiters, rovers, landers, and Deep Space Network dishes, and can switch the Moon and Mars between imagery and laser-altimeter elevation. In the Ground station stage, they point a DSN dish at the actual current hour and rebuild a real NASA terrain photo by majority voting.

Made by a team with different ideas. The original idea came from a brainstorm by the three of us. Mission 3's signal-encoding game is based on Jeongha's design, and Operation Deep Link, her Deep Space Network training game, is now part of the campaign. Each crew member takes a role, so a class works as a mission team.

Friendly but not childish. CAPCOM Whiskers, the cat guide, explains terms and results in plain language. The soundtrack is inspired by the Voyager Golden Record, but because the record's music is still under copyright, we use an original ambient score that is generated live instead.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy. Orbit physics is tested against real missions (LRO, Gateway NRHO, MRO, MAVEN, MESSENGER, Dawn). The Moon terrain was sampled in two independent ways and the results matched exactly. A robot player wins every Moon objective and the hardest Mars objective with sensible rovers, while badly designed rovers fail, so the game is neither impossible nor trivial.

Honesty about simplification. Sunlight, ice amounts, Earth visibility, Mars heights, noise, and costs are simplified game models, and the game labels them as such.

Data provenance and licensing. The Briefing Room lists each NASA source with its Open Data Portal entry and the licence the catalogue states. We used NASA 3D models and NASA audio that NASA publishes freely, avoided copyrighted music, and did not use or alter NASA logos or mission identifiers.

Audience and classrooms. The game is written for ages 12 to first-year university. Class mode fits a whole campaign into a 45-minute lesson, and teachers get a lesson plan, discussion questions, a printable worksheet, and a CSV export. Tooltips and an automatic glossary explain space terms, and Mission 1 has a guided tutorial.

Slower school laptops. A Graphics setting offers Auto, High, and Lite. Auto starts sharp and drops to Lite if the frame rate stays low. Lite renders at 1x resolution with no shadows or animated backgrounds and caps at 30 fps. 3D views pause when offscreen or in a background tab, and planet icons use small thumbnails instead of full-size maps.

Privacy. There are no accounts. Crew profiles and decision history are stored only in the browser, and Ask CAPCOM runs offline. The optional AI advisor is off by default and only ever receives mission numbers.

Ease of use. The game can be played from the keyboard (press / for Ask CAPCOM and ? for settings), and nothing needs to be installed.

Sputnik beeps: The NASA audio page lists Apollo 11 but not Sputnik. The game's Briefing Room only says "nasa.gov audio collection" for the Sputnik beeps and gives no page, so I can't confirm where they came from. If you know the exact NASA page, add a row for it. If not, row 10 is still correct for the Apollo 11 clips, and the Briefing Room's "nasa.gov audio collection" wording will do for Sputnik.

- ESA data: the Mars map also uses ESA's Mars Express HRSC data. That goes in the "Space Agency Partner & Other Data" table, not here.

- Mission design resources: NASA's "Design and Develop Science Missions", JPL's "Concept Maturity Levels", GSFC's "Mission Design Lab" and GMAT are listed in your README as challenge resources. I couldn't find their URLs. Add them as extra rows only if you have the links. The text I wrote only says the physics starts from the same first step as GMAT, so leaving them out is fine.
